{{Short description|Mathematical bound}}
{{about|determinants of matrices|statistical block design theory|Fisher's inequality}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Fischer's inequality''' gives an upper bound for the [[determinant]] of a [[Positive-definite matrix | positive-semidefinite matrix]] whose entries are complex numbers in terms of the determinants of its principal diagonal blocks. 
Suppose ''A'', ''C'' are respectively ''p''&times;''p'', ''q''&times;''q'' positive-semidefinite complex matrices and ''B'' is a ''p''&times;''q'' complex matrix.
Let 
:<math>M := \left[\begin{matrix} A & B \\ B^* & C \end{matrix}\right]</math> 
so that ''M'' is a (''p''+''q'')&times;(''p''+''q'') matrix.

Then Fischer's inequality states that 
:<math> \det (M) \le \det(A) \det(C).</math> 
If ''M'' is positive-definite, equality is achieved in Fischer's inequality if and only if all the entries of ''B'' are 0. Inductively one may conclude that a similar inequality holds for a block decomposition of ''M'' with multiple principal diagonal blocks. Considering 1&times;1 blocks, a corollary is [[Hadamard's inequality]]. On the other hand, Fischer's inequality can also be proved by using Hadamard's inequality, see the proof of Theorem 7.8.5 in Horn and Johnson's [[Matrix analysis|Matrix Analysis]].

==Proof==
Assume that ''A'' and ''C'' are positive-definite. We have <math>A^{-1}</math> and <math>C^{-1}</math> are positive-definite. Let 
:<math>D := \left[\begin{matrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & C \end{matrix}\right].</math> 
We note that
:<math>D^{-\frac{1}{2}} M D^{-\frac{1}{2} } = \left[\begin{matrix} A^{-\frac{1}{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & C^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{matrix}\right] \left[\begin{matrix} A & B \\ B^* & C \end{matrix}\right] \left[\begin{matrix} A^{-\frac{1}{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & C^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{matrix}\right] = \left[\begin{matrix} I_{p} & A^{-\frac{1}{2}} BC^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ C^{-\frac{1}{2}}B^*A^{-\frac{1}{2}} & I_{q}\end{matrix}\right]</math>
Applying the [[inequality of arithmetic and geometric means | AM-GM inequality]] to the eigenvalues of <math>D^{-\frac{1}{2}} M D^{-\frac{1}{2} }</math>, we see
:<math>\det (D^{-\frac{1}{2}} M D^{-\frac{1}{2}}) \le \left({1 \over p + q} \mathrm{tr} (D^{-\frac{1}{2}} M D^{-\frac{1}{2}}) \right)^{p+q} = 1^{p+q} = 1.</math>
By multiplicativity of [[determinant]], we have 
:<math>
\begin{align}
\det(D^{-\frac{1}{2}} ) \det(M) \det(D^{-\frac{1}{2}} ) \le 1 \\
\Longrightarrow \det(M) \le \det(D) = \det(A) \det(C).
\end{align}</math>
In this case, equality holds if and only if ''M'' = ''D'' that is, all entries of ''B'' are 0.

For <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, as <math>A + \varepsilon I_p</math> and <math>C + \varepsilon I_q</math> are positive-definite, we have 
:<math>\det(M+ \varepsilon I_{p+q}) \le \det(A + \varepsilon I_p) \det(C + \varepsilon I_q).</math>

Taking the limit as <math>\varepsilon \rightarrow 0</math> proves the inequality. From the inequality we note that if ''M'' is invertible, then both ''A'' and ''C'' are invertible and we get the desired equality condition.

== Improvements ==
If ''M'' can be partitioned in square blocks ''M<sub>ij</sub>'', then the following inequality by Thompson is valid:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Thompson|first=R. C.|title=A determinantal inequality for positive definite matrices|journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]]|volume=4|pages=57–62|doi=10.4153/cmb-1961-010-9|doi-access=free|year=1961}}</ref>

: <math>\det(M) \leq \det([\det(M_{ij})])  </math>

where [det(''M<sub>ij</sub>'')] is the matrix whose (''i'',''j'') entry is det(''M<sub>ij</sub>'').

In particular, if the block matrices ''B'' and ''C'' are also square matrices, then the following inequality by Everett is valid:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Everitt|first=W. N.|title=A note on positive definite matrices|journal=Glasgow Mathematical Journal|volume=3|issue=4|pages=173–175|doi=10.1017/S2040618500033670|issn=2051-2104|year=1958|doi-access=free}}</ref>

: <math>\det(M) \le \det \begin{bmatrix} \det(A) && \det(B) \\ \det(B^*) && \det(C) \end{bmatrix}</math>

Thompson's inequality can also be generalized by an inequality in terms of the coefficients of the [[characteristic polynomial]] of the block matrices. Expressing the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ''A'' as

: <math>p_A (t) = \sum_{k=0}^n t^{n-k} (-1)^k \operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^k A)</math>

and supposing that the blocks ''M<sub>ij</sub>'' are ''m'' x ''m'' matrices, the following inequality by Lin and Zhang is valid:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lin|first=Minghua|last2=Zhang|first2=Pingping|title=Unifying a result of Thompson and a result of Fiedler and Markham on block positive definite matrices|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=533|pages=380–385|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2017.07.032|year=2017|doi-access=free}}</ref>

: <math>\det(M) \le \left(\frac{\det([\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^r M_{ij}]))}{ \binom{m}r} \right)^{\frac{m}{r}},\quad r=1, \ldots, m</math>

Note that if ''r'' = ''m'', then this inequality is identical to Thompson's inequality.
